title: Faith
hook: the first theological virtue: trust in God, a gift that grows

segments.voice: Yesterday, do not covet: the commandment about wanting what's your neighbor's. Your line was enough is enough. What did you find on your own side of the fence? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

A father has brought his sick son to Jesus's disciples, and they couldn't help. Now Jesus is here, and the father says, if thou canst do any thing, help us. Jesus picks up that little word if. All things are possible, he says, to him that believeth. And the father, in Mark's Gospel, cries out with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Belief and unbelief in one breath, and Jesus heals the boy. Today begins a new stretch: three gifts Christian teachers call the theological virtues. The first in Paul's list is the one the father was holding onto with both hands. Faith.

Paul names the three together at the end of his passage on love: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three." Christian teachers came to call them theological virtues, because they're aimed at God, and tradition says they're given by God rather than built by effort alone. The Greek word the New Testament uses for faith, pistis, also means trust. That matters. Faith here is less a list of ideas you sign and more a hand you put in someone else's. The letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." It leans on what can't yet be seen. And it's called a gift. Ephesians says: "by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Christians read that weight differently. Lutheran and Reformed churches tend to stress that last line: through faith, a gift, not earned. Catholic and Orthodox churches tend to stress, with Galatians, faith which worketh by love. Both read both verses. And a gift can grow. In Luke's Gospel the apostles ask Jesus, "Increase our faith." He answers that faith even as small as a grain of mustard seed could tell a tree to be uprooted and planted in the sea. Which brings us back to the father. He didn't wait until his doubt was gone. He brought it along, said so out loud, and asked for help with it. In the story, that was enough to begin.

Here's the practice: trust one thing to God. Settle, and breathe. Find one worry you've been carrying in a closed fist: a child, a test result, money, a decision. Name it plainly. Then, slowly, open your actual hands on your knees, palms up. If you pray, you can hand it over in the father's words: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If you don't pray, just let your hands stay open, and notice what it's like not to grip. The bell holds the time.
Faith. In the New Testament's Greek, pistis: trust in God. Christians call it a gift, and something that can grow.
Your line: trust. Today, when the worry you named comes back, open one hand, even inside a pocket, and let it be held for a minute. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Christians speak of faith as trust in God that is given and grows; in some churches they profess it together in a creed on Sundays, and some pray the father's words from Mark 9:24 or the apostles' 'increase our faith' in hard moments.

fork.setup: you're the father. Jesus has just said all things are possible to him that believeth, and you know your own heart is divided. what do you say?
options: I believe completely; I have no doubts.
Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
nothing; you walk away until your doubt is gone.
fork.reveal: he says both at once, with tears, and Jesus heals the boy. the story honors honest faith that asks for help.

original.note: Greek: faith, trust, the word used throughout the New Testament for faith.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means being sure.
what it means: trust in God, given as a gift, that can grow, and can live alongside doubt.
what a scholar hears: pistis covers faith and trust in one word, and Hebrews 11:1 ties it to things hoped for and not yet seen.
recall: gathering in silence, waiting on God

notes: Index hook calls faith 'the first theological virtue'; the script grounds 'first' only in the order of Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 13:13.
'Theological virtues' attributed to 'Christian teachers' and 'tradition says they're given by God' (infused virtues, e.g. Aquinas); confirm the phrasing.
Protestant / Catholic and Orthodox emphasis (Ephesians 2:8 vs Galatians 5:6) described as emphasis only, with 'many Protestant churches'; confirm it is fair to all three.
Mark 9:22–23 paraphrased ('if thou canst do any thing'; 'all things are possible to him that believeth'). 'Couldn't help' summarizes 9:18.
Luke 17:6 paraphrased: faith as a grain of mustard seed could say to a sycamine tree, be plucked up; confirm 'move a tree' summary.

Editor pass: Luke 17:6 summary 'enough to move a tree' made closer to the text (a sycamine tree told to be plucked up and planted in the sea); howItsDone's creeds line limited to 'some churches', since not every church recites a creed.
Audit pass: church emphases softened to 'tend to stress' so neither side is reduced to one verse; Keeper to confirm the Orthodox framing via Galatians 5:6 is fair.
